blogs.title: Faster LLM inference startup: What you need to know
blogs.content: Posted on November 6, 2026 by Baofa Fan, DaoCloud CNCF projects highlighted in this post Adding an inference replica creates capacity only after the new instance can serve requests. Between starting a process and generating a response, an LLM server may need to load weights, initialize GPU resources, compile kernels, capture execution graphs, and warm up the engine. Restarts, model switches, and scale-out can repeat this work. The community is addressing these costs at several levels. vLLM and SGLang are developing ways to reuse weights and initialized state. Serving platforms are building workflows around warm instances and snapshots. Kubernetes, container runtimes, and the Open Container Initiative (OCI) are working on related interfaces and artifact questions. These efforts have different boundaries and are progressing independently. Understanding what each approach preserves helps explain both its benefits and its current scope. Why starting an inference server takes time A typical startup includes several kinds of work. The server launches processes and imports libraries. It reads model files, constructs tensors, and performs any required weight transformations. It initializes the execution runtime and communication between workers, allocates memory, and prepares the engine to serve. Some work happens specifically to improve subsequent inference performance. Compilation produces executable kernels; autotuning selects implementations for a configuration. CUDA Graph capture records GPU operations for later replay with lower launch overhead. The vLLM optimization documentation describes the tradeoff between startup work and steady-state execution performance. The balance depends on the model, software, hardware, and storage. Once model files are cached locally, engine initialization may become more visible. Once weights can be reused in GPU memory, imports, tuning, and graph capture may account for more of the remaining delay. What can be reused instead of rebuilt Startup optimizations can be grouped by the work they preserve: What is reused Approach Representative projects or features Work that can remain Model files Pre-staging and efficient loaders llm-d model caches, fastsafetensors Weight processing and initialization Compiled artifacts and tuning results Persistent caches vLLM compilation and autotune caches Runtime setup and graph capture Processed weights Daemons and weight transfer vLLM preload, SGLang weight cache, ModelExpress Construction of the rest of the engine A live engine Sleep/wake and warm instances vLLM sleep, SGLang memory saver, llm-d FMA Restoring released resources Initialized execution state Engine or container snapshots vLLM snapshots, SGLang snapshot proposal, Snapshot, llm-d/GKE Validation, restoration, and recovery work These approaches can appear together in a system, with integration conditions specific to each implementation. For example, an engine might reuse compiled artifacts while loading weights through a specialized loader. A snapshot workflow might discard an empty key/value (KV) cache before capture and recreate it after restoration. This cache holds attention state computed while processing tokens. Efficient loading remains a separate area of work. SGLang documents loaders such as pre-sharded state, fastsafetensors, and streaming loaders. llm-d documents model-file caches alongside other startup paths. These mechanisms affect how weights reach an engine; they preserve different states from a snapshot of an initialized process. SGLang model loading , llm-d startup overview . What vLLM and SGLang are doing vLLM vLLM’s Fast Start work centers on a persistent weight daemon. It loads and processes weights, holds the resulting tensors in GPU memory, and exposes them to compatible engines through CUDA inter-process communication. The weight-daemon implementation and the vllm preload command have been merged. Current preload documentation also describes preparing FlashInfer autotune results before an engine starts. Fast Start implementation , preload documentation . This separates the lifetime of cached weights from an engine restart. In the zero-copy mode, an engine maps the daemon’s existing allocations. Configuration checks determine whether reuse is appropriate, and the documented path can fall back to ordinary loading. The daemon must remain alive while engines use its memory. CUDA IPC handles are local to a node; documented multi-node deployments provide the relevant shards locally on each node. vLLM also has sleep/wake support, which retains a live server while releasing much of its GPU memory. That provides a different lifecycle from starting a new engine against cached weights. The preload documentation identifies restrictions on combining its zero-copy mode with weight offloading through sleep mode. Sleep mode . A separate, merged implementation adds experimental initialized-engine snapshots. The vllm snapshot workflow uses CRIU to capture and restore Linux process state, with CUDA checkpoint support handling GPU state. Its documented scope requires the same machine and compatible environment, with one NVIDIA GPU and tensor parallelism of one. It releases weights and KV state before capture and reloads them during restoration, retaining a dependency on the model files. Restoration also checks a recorded generation result. Initialized engine snapshots . SGLang SGLang has merged a weight-cache daemon that holds processed weights and shares them with new engine instances through CUDA IPC. Its Fast Engine Recovery roadmap discusses extending this foundation, including broader model and quantization coverage, memory transport, daemon lifecycle, and remaining initialization costs. The roadmap describes directions beyond the merged initial implementation. Weight-cache implementation , Fast Engine Recovery roadmap . SGLang also exposes memory release/resume and generation pause/continue operations used by external snapshot integrations. Whether weights remain available after release depends on the configured memory policy, including CPU backup. These operations let integrations prepare an engine for capture and resume it afterward; the surrounding workflow still needs to coordinate them. Initialized-engine snapshots are another direction. The open RFC and implementation PR propose capturing SGLang after initialization and before its HTTP service binds. Their initial scope is one NVIDIA GPU, tensor parallelism of one, and the same host and software environment. Model weights remain external and are reloaded after restore. Initialization snapshot RFC , implementation PR . Both frameworks also have open proposals about cooperating with an external checkpoint orchestrator. The engine would prepare its own state and resume serving; the external system would capture, store, and restore the process. These proposals address a practical boundary: a node agent can operate checkpoint tools, while the inference engine knows when its requests, caches, and communication resources are safe to capture. vLLM proposal , SGLang proposal . How platforms turn mechanisms into startup workflows Snapshot and Dynamo The independent Snapshot project in the ai-dynamo organization provides checkpoint and restore primitives for GPU workloads on Kubernetes. Its operator and node agent coordinate CRIU and CUDA checkpoint operations, with resources such as PodSnapshot and SnapshotJob. Dynamo integrates these primitives into its serving workflows. Snapshot project . Snapshot’s documented storage path uses a shared persistent volume accessible by node agents. Agent-side components manage artifact movement and restore access. Its current storage documentation supports storage through a Kubernetes PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC); object-storage backends are reserved for future use. Hardware, driver, runtime, and workload compatibility still constrain restoration. Storage model . The framework examples also show the application work ...
